title: Tutankhamun's tomb, 1922 — one last season, one step in the sand
sources: Wikipedia: Howard Carter — by 1922 Lord Carnarvon was dissatisfied with the lack of results after several years and considered withdrawing his funding, then agreed to fund one more season in the Valley of the Kings; on 4 November 1922 a worker uncovered a step in the rock (other accounts credit a boy digging outside the assigned area); Carter had the steps dug until a sealed, mud-plastered doorway appeared, refilled the staircase and telegraphed Carnarvon, who arrived on 23 November; on 26 November Carter made a tiny breach in the doorway with a chisel his grandmother had given him for his 17th birthday, and peered in by candlelight; Carnarvon asked 'Can you see anything?' and Carter replied 'Yes, wonderful things!' (his journal records 'Yes, it is wonderful'); the tomb was virtually intact and contained over 5,000 items, the best preserved pharaonic tomb ever found in the Valley; Carnarvon contracted blood poisoning and died in Cairo on 5 April 1923
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1890 the City and South London Railway opens; 1979 Iranian students seize the US embassy in Tehran, beginning a 444-day hostage crisis

Photos (public domain / CC0): Harry Burton's photographs of the tomb (antechamber, the Anubis shrine, the corridor, the excavation, carrying out the finds, Carter at the coffin); Carter, Carnarvon and Lady Evelyn at the tomb; Lord Carnarvon; the gold mask in Cairo and in Burton's photograph; the tomb sign, KV62
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a candle in the dark, desert sand

post.facebook:
On this day in 1922, a worker in Egypt's Valley of the Kings uncovered a single step in the rock.

Howard Carter had been searching for years, and his patron, Lord Carnarvon, had nearly given up — he agreed to fund just one more season. Now the step led down to more steps, and to a sealed doorway. Carter filled the stairs back in and telegraphed Carnarvon in England.

On 26 November, with Carnarvon beside him, Carter made a tiny hole in the door with a chisel his grandmother had given him, held up a candle, and looked in. "Can you see anything?" Carnarvon asked. "Yes," Carter answered, "wonderful things."

It was the tomb of the boy-king Tutankhamun — almost untouched, with more than 5,000 objects inside, including his mask of solid gold. Five months later, Lord Carnarvon died of blood poisoning in Cairo.

Also on 4 November: London's City and South London Railway opened (1890), and the Tehran hostage crisis began (1979).

youtube.description:
4 November 1922: after years of finding almost nothing, Howard Carter was in his last funded season when a worker uncovered a step in the Valley of the Kings. It led down to a sealed doorway. Three weeks later Carter chipped a hole with his grandmother's chisel and looked in by candlelight. "Can you see anything?" asked Lord Carnarvon. "Yes, wonderful things." It was Tutankhamun's tomb — almost intact, with more than 5,000 objects and a solid gold mask. Five months later, Carnarvon was dead.

Also on 4 November: the City and South London Railway (1890) and the Tehran hostage crisis (1979).
